Hi Donisha,

On Mon, Jul 20, 2020 at 9:00 PM Donisha Smith <dsmi...@fiu.edu> wrote:
Hi all,

As the title states, I am a first year graduate student and am currently attempting to conduct data analysis for my Master's project. I haven't taken many courses so I had to resort to studying item response theory on my own. My goal is to obtain valid scores from an anxiety assessment, which was administered at pre-treatment and post-treatment,so is a repeated measure, to use in linear mixed model and assess gender differences in anxiety at baseline and analyze potential gender differences in anxiety changes over time. So, because I am a novice, I wanted to draw on someone's expertise with the mirt package to ensure thatI am using the package correctly:

1) From my understanding of irt with polytomous, item difficulties are the average of the observed responses divided by the maximum possible response.

That's perhaps a definition based on observations only, and sounds more akin to what one would find in classical test theory item analyses. In IRT difficulty/intercept parameters are estimated from a model given the available response data, so you won't get this type of definition.
 
Let's say I have 20 items in my assessment, all which have a maximum of 4 categories with 0 being the lowest, but at baseline, participants are less likely to endorse higher categories, how exactly do I use the customK function to let the package the true total number of categories in each question?

You could supply the value of 5 to the customK function for these items, but I would highly advise against this. Categories not observed are not identifiable, so if you tried to estimate the parameters associated with missing categories you'll obtain meaningless parameters, and the model will fail to converge.
 

2) I'm aware that if I want to compare participants across time, I have to ensure measurement invariance, where items are functioning similarly among participants with the similar latent abilities; however, because my ultimate goal is to compare gender differences across time. My idea is to conduct differential item functioning between males and females at baseline, eliminate items that show a gender bias, then conduct differential item functioning between  the baseline group (combined male and female) with themselves at post treatment to eliminate longitudinal item bias. I have looked at the literature extensively but most studies either perform DIF between groups only or perform DIF across time only. So, I wanted to know if my idea is reasonable.

The idea seems reasonable enough to me if this is indeed your research purpose.
 

3) From my understanding, anchoring items for DIF can result in misleading fit statistics; however, is the opposite true? Where undercutting items can lead to a poor DIF analysis? Since the DIF and the multipleGroup function identifies 'n' number of groups and scales the groups to be equated for DIF. I believe that I should first conduct separate/individual single class models for baseline males and females and analyze item fits separately for both group and select the overlapping "good" fitting items to use in baseline DIF for males and females and to use in the longitudinal DIF.

That's also reasonable. You wouldn't want to compare groups across anchored models if within the groups the models fit poorly. 
 

4) (I promise this is the last question). I also have a bit of missing data in my pre condition and my post condition (approximately 4% in each). My idea was to conduct conduct the baseline and longitudinal DIF first and once I can assure that all items have good fit and display no bias, then I can use the imputeMissing function on the longitudinal multipleGroup model with anchored intercepts and slopes to  generate the missing scores.

Missing data shouldn't pose much of an issue in mirt since the estimation algorithms are all full-information based. Unless you have outside information about how to plausibly generate the response absent the fitted IRT models then it's best to just leave the missing data as-is and rely on assumptions such as 'missing at random'.
 

Admittedly, I have been experimenting with the package extensively and have been adjusting the latent distribution since their is evidence that the distribution is non normal and conducting DIF(which.par = c('a1', 'd'), scheme = 'drop') to analyze the slope and intercepts jointly. But I'm not entirely confident in my analysis plan. Some of you are probably wondering why I don't ask my mentor but I am in a neuroscience program so many do not emphasize the behavioral statistics. Additionally, due to the epidemic, professors in different departments haven't been responding to my requests. I just want to construct a reliable behavioral model so that I can transition into creating a neural model knowing that my behavioral model is valid.

Trying times for all. Good luck.

Phil
 

Thanks! I apologize for the essay. Also, any excellent resources would be helpful. I have already purchased about two different textbooks.
